problem.title: Pump failure prediction
problem.context: A water utility operates about 400 pumps at 12 stations. Vibration, temperature, and pressure sensors report every second; rural stations have unreliable mobile connections. The utility has two data scientists and depends on IT for servers and networks.

requirements.text: Warn the maintenance team at least 24 hours before a pump is likely to fail, naming the pump and the probable cause.
Improve the predictions as technicians record what they find at each inspection.
When a station loses its connection for up to two days, warnings for its pumps still reach the station's on-call technician.
When a new pump model is installed, its pumps get predictions within one month, without changes to how the other pumps are scored.
Sensor data stays on the utility's own premises: no cloud service may store or process it.

points.description: 1. The application contains the model as a module in a modular monolith, using a shared data store and a local service/API for real-time predictions. Streamed inputs are collected and processed into batches for training; clients receive push notifications when results are available, while MLOps and CI/CD build, test, and deploy models and other components. 2. Trade-off: This provides integrated, automated delivery and responsive serving while accommodating batch training. It gives up fully automatic model adaptation, since monitoring-triggered changes require human adjustment and redeployment, and the shared monolith/store can reduce deployment or scaling independence.

Continuous input is streamed and stored as events, which an event-driven model service consumes for incremental training. A microservice serves real-time predictions and pushes results to clients, while an MLOps orchestrator and CI/CD pipelines build, test, deploy, and monitor the components, triggering automated model adjustments. Trade-off: This gains decoupling, traceability, real-time responsiveness, and automated delivery, but increases distributed-system and operational complexity. Incremental learning and automated adjustment can also introduce model instability or unintended changes without effective monitoring and controls.

Batch data is ingested into a shared data store, models are trained offline, and an external batch prediction system processes scheduled data and writes scores back to that store. Clients poll for results, while humans monitor outcomes, adjust models, and redeploy them using manually invoked build and deployment scripts without MLOps or CI/CD deployment automation. Trade-off: This favors simple, scheduled operations and shared access, but sacrifices low-latency results, event-driven notification, and automated model adjustment and delivery; polling and manual steps increase delay and operational effort.

The modular monolith ingests a continuous stream into a shared store; new training data triggers an automated pipeline that trains, evaluates, and validates models in batches. CI/CD builds, tests, and deploys the model and other components; a local API serves predictions and push notifications report results, while MLOps supports monitoring and human model adjustment. Trade-off: This provides repeatable delivery and timely result notification, but shared storage and monolithic/local serving limit independent scaling, while batch training and manual adjustment slow adaptation to drift.

1. An event-driven application ingests continuous data, stores it as events, and sends it through pub/sub or queues to a locally served model. Incremental training, automated adjustment, and push notifications provide continuously updated predictions, while MLOps orchestration and CI/CD build, test, and deploy the required pipelines and components. 2. Trade-off: This enables responsive, continuously improving operation and reproducible automation, but increases infrastructure and operational complexity. Automated adjustments and incremental learning also heighten risks from drift, noisy feedback, or unintended model changes, requiring monitoring and governance.

The system ingests continuous streams into an event store and exposes model services through event-driven queues or pub/sub. An MLOps orchestrator, with CI/CD building and deploying pipeline components, supports hybrid batch/online training and serving; clients receive prediction results through push notifications, while humans adjust models based on monitoring. Trade-off: This enables responsive predictions, replayable data, and flexible batch/incremental learning, but increases orchestration and operational complexity. Manual model adjustment limits automation and can delay responses to monitoring findings.

The application contains the model as a modular-monolith module, using a shared data store and local API to serve predictions. Streaming inputs are stored and versioned in the code repository; newly available training data triggers a batch training, evaluation, and validation pipeline, while clients receive push notifications and production data and predictions are monitored. Trade-off: MLOps and CI/CD automate reproducible model and component delivery, but batch training delays adaptation to changing data. Manual adjustment preserves human control but adds operational effort and slows responses to monitoring findings.

Streaming data is captured in an event store and delivered through an event-driven pub/sub or queue interface to a locally served model API; prediction availability is pushed to clients. An MLOps orchestrator coordinates model building, hybrid batch/incremental training, monitoring-triggered automated adjustment, and CI/CD pipelines that build, test, and deploy the required components. Trade-off: This provides responsive processing, decoupled integration, and automated delivery and adaptation, but increases orchestration and operational complexity; mixed training modes and automated adjustments require careful control and validation.

An event-driven application ingests continuous data through streams, records exchanged data in an event store, and invokes model services through pub/sub or queues. An MLOps orchestrator automates training, evaluation, validation, hybrid batch/incremental learning, monitoring-triggered adjustment, and CI/CD deployment; hybrid serving computes predictions online and offline, then pushes results to clients. Trade-off: This supports responsive predictions, reproducibility, automation, and adaptation while combining real-time and batch workloads. It gives up architectural simplicity, requiring coordination across event infrastructure, pipelines, model versions, monitoring, and potentially more operational resources.

approaches.idea: What if local modular serving and controlled batch retraining kept the system manageable while serving station users?
What if an event-driven system learned and adjusted continuously from incoming sensor and technician data?
What if scheduled batch scoring and manual operations minimized architectural demands?
approaches.dropped_because: Batch-only scoring with polling and no automated deployment gives up timely, resilient warning delivery and rapid support for a newly installed pump model.

approaches.idea: What if hybrid online and offline serving combined fast predictions with batch processing and hybrid learning?

trajectory.hypothesis: A local serving path with pushed alerts should support timely pump warnings and station operations; batch training and manual adjustment may incorporate inspection findings more slowly, while automated delivery may help add new pump models.

tradeoffs.note: Local real-time serving and push notification can get predictions to a station promptly, but the values do not specify buffering, durable local delivery, or what happens to notifications during a two-day outage.
Batch training with human adjustment offers a controlled route for incorporating inspection findings, but it delays adaptation compared with automated adjustment.

trajectory.observation: The checked combination has no warnings or unmet requirements and no sources attest it. The local serving path is promising for rural operation, but the point does not guarantee offline notification or prediction horizon and cause accuracy.

trajectory.hypothesis: Event storage and continuous learning should make sensor and inspection events available for adaptation; microservice serving and push notifications should produce timely predictions, while automation helps onboard a pump model.

tradeoffs.note: Distributed real-time serving and push delivery favor quick alerts, but do not specify local operation or notification buffering when a station loses its mobile connection.
Incremental learning and automatic adjustment can rapidly use new inspection data, but add controls and validation work that complicate safe onboarding of a new pump model.

trajectory.observation: The combination checks cleanly but is unattested. Its event history and automation support ongoing adaptation, while the distributed service and automated model changes add operational and model-control burden for a small team.

trajectory.hypothesis: Scheduled batch scoring with polling should be straightforward to operate, but may miss the warning lead time, station availability and modular pump-model onboarding scenarios.

tradeoffs.note: Scheduled batch scores and polling simplify the flow, but offer no defined timely local alert delivery and no automated route to independent pump-model onboarding.

trajectory.observation: The point checks cleanly but is a poor fit for the most constraining warning and availability scenarios. The shared store does not establish that sensor data remains on premises, and manual steps do not support the one-month onboarding target well enough.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding a model-building pipeline triggered when technician findings become training data should improve repeatability of learning from inspections and make the model workflow easier to extend for another pump model.

tradeoffs.note: An automated batch pipeline can reproducibly retrain after new inspection data arrives, but batch retraining still adds delay before learning is reflected in predictions and does not guarantee the one-month target.

trajectory.observation: The pipeline makes the feedback and deployment path more explicit, while keeping local inference and human oversight. The design space does not specify an update interval or guarantee the one-month target. The point is unattested and checks without warnings.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing distributed microservice serving with a local service should retain event-driven learning and modular delivery while bringing inference closer to rural stations and reducing dependence on mobile connectivity.

tradeoffs.note: Local serving improves the chance that a station can continue scoring during a link loss, but the local service value does not itself provide store-and-forward alert delivery or independent deployment of pump-specific models.
Continuous learning from findings can adapt predictions quickly, but requires careful model validation and version control as new pump models are introduced.

trajectory.observation: The local API closes part of the rural-operation gap while retaining event-driven feedback. Offline notification delivery and a one-month onboarding guarantee remain unspecified. No sources attest the point; it checks cleanly.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid online/offline serving and hybrid learning may combine quick predictions with batch work and reuse of technician findings, retaining event history and push notifications.

tradeoffs.note: Online paths support quick scoring and batch paths support broader learning, but coordinating two serving and training modes adds complexity to pump-model onboarding.
Human review supports controlled model changes but can slow the use of inspection findings.

trajectory.observation: The hybrid path offers flexibility across online and offline workloads, but coordination across paths and human adjustment create operational overhead. The combination checks cleanly and is unattested.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding versioned training records and production logging should make inspection feedback and model behavior easier to trace without changing the local-serving architecture.

tradeoffs.note: Versioning and logging improve traceability for feedback and model changes, but add repository and monitoring practices that the small team must maintain.

trajectory.observation: Monitoring and versioned records make the retraining path more reviewable, and the combination remains cleanly checked. The space does not guarantee forecast accuracy, a 24-hour lead, or a specific onboarding duration; it describes the surrounding workflow rather than the prediction method.

trajectory.hypothesis: Using a dedicated model-builder component and hybrid training should keep pump-model work modular while balancing rapid updates with batch validation, reducing some risk of fully incremental changes.

tradeoffs.note: A separate builder component and hybrid learning can support controlled updates from findings, but orchestration and validation still require team capacity for the one-month onboarding goal.
Automated adjustment can use findings promptly but raises the amount of monitoring and governance needed for safe new-model rollout.

trajectory.observation: Hybrid training and a dedicated builder preserve modularity while moderating the continuously incremental seed. The local API still only partly addresses station-side alert availability; the checked point has no warnings and no attesting sources.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing manual adjustment with automated adjustment and explicitly building, testing, and deploying the model pipeline should reduce the time to use technician findings and support model onboarding in the hybrid design.

tradeoffs.note: Automation shortens the path from new findings or model code to updated predictions, but adds release-control and monitoring work for the small team.

trajectory.observation: Automated adjustment and broader CI/CD improve repeatability and response speed but increase operational demands. Hybrid online/offline coordination remains the main cost; the point checks without warnings and is unattested.

alternatives.name: Local modular prediction with controlled retraining
alternatives.summary: Serve predictions from a local API, stream sensor data, and use versioned batch retraining from new inspection data with monitored, human-reviewed changes. This reduces dependence on central connectivity while keeping the workflow familiar to a small team.

choices.reason: A model module within a modular monolith gives the new pump-model work a defined module boundary.
A shared store can hold sensor history and inspection findings for retraining; its location must be configured on premises.
A local real-time API can score pumps near the station when the mobile link is down.
choices.fit_note: Local serving does not define the forecasting method, 24-hour horizon, probable-cause inference, or durable offline notification path.

choices.reason: Push notification provides a direct alerting mechanism.
choices.fit_note: The value does not specify local notification transport, buffering, or delivery guarantees during a two-day link outage.

choices.reason: Continuous ingestion makes the one-second sensor reports available to the prediction workflow.

A model-building pipeline automates training, evaluation, and validation.
Batch learning gives a controlled route to incorporate inspection labels.
Logging data and predictions helps trace behavior after updates.
Human review retains control over changes based on monitoring and new findings.
MLOps supports repeatable monitoring and model workflow practices.

Build, test, and deploy automation includes served models and system components.

alternatives.name: Event-driven, continuously adapting prediction
alternatives.summary: Capture data and feedback as events, serve locally through an event-driven model interface, and use hybrid learning with automated adjustment and orchestrated delivery. It favors fast adaptation and decoupled components at the cost of operational complexity.

choices.reason: An event-driven model interface fits continuous sensor and inspection events.
An event store preserves the stream of sensor and technician events for replay and learning.
Local API serving brings inference to the station while retaining event-driven integration.
choices.fit_note: Local serving does not define the prediction horizon, probable-cause method, or durable offline notification delivery.

choices.reason: Push notification makes new warnings available without requiring routine polling.
choices.fit_note: The space does not say how pushes are buffered or delivered across a station's lost connection.

choices.reason: Streamed ingestion matches continuous sensor readings.

considered.reason: Distributed microservice serving was tried first; local serving better supports disconnected stations.
Pure incremental learning was set aside in favor of hybrid learning with a batch validation path.

alternatives.name: Hybrid online and batch prediction
alternatives.summary: Combine event-driven online serving with offline batch work and hybrid training, with CI/CD and automated monitoring adjustments. This spans fast and large-scale workloads but has the highest coordination burden.

choices.reason: Event-driven integration carries sensor and feedback data through the system.
An event store retains inputs and findings for online and offline workflows.
Hybrid serving combines online calculations with offline batch calculations.
choices.fit_note: The online path can support timely scoring, but this value does not promise local execution, outage buffering, or a specific 24-hour predictive horizon.

choices.reason: Push notification announces available warnings.
choices.fit_note: No delivery guarantee or offline notification path is defined.

choices.reason: Streamed ingestion receives continuous sensor data and technician events.

Hybrid learning balances quick adjustment with batch learning.

adrs.title: Prediction serving and warning delivery
adrs.context: The utility needs pump-specific warnings in time to act and needs them to reach station technicians during mobile outages. Local or hybrid prediction paths and push notification help with responsiveness, but the design space does not define the forecasting model, warning horizon, probable-cause explanation, station-local buffering, or delivery guarantees.

options.name: Local modular serving
pros: Local real-time serving can continue without a central mobile connection.
Streaming inputs and push notifications support prompt workflows.
cons: The design space does not establish the predictive horizon, cause identification, or durable offline notification delivery.
options.reason: Choose this when operational simplicity and station-proximate inference are priorities.

options.name: Event-driven local serving
pros: Decoupled event integration fits continuous sensor and inspection inputs.
Local serving reduces dependence on a remote inference service.
cons: Event infrastructure and automated changes increase operating and governance demands; outage alert delivery remains unspecified.
options.reason: Choose this for fast feedback and component separation when the utility can support the added operating complexity.

options.name: Hybrid online and offline serving
pros: Combines online prediction with offline batch calculations.
Event-driven inputs and push notification cover continuous workflows.
cons: Coordination between online and offline paths increases complexity and does not guarantee station-side alert delivery during an outage.
options.reason: Choose this where both responsive calculation and batch processing are important and the team can manage two paths.

options.name: Scheduled batch polling
pros: Scheduled batch processing and polling have a straightforward operating flow.
cons: The point misses the timely warning and disconnected-station scenarios.
options.reason: Set aside because scheduled output and polling do not support the urgent warning and availability drivers.

adrs.title: Learning from inspections and onboarding pump models
adrs.context: Inspection findings must improve predictions, and a new pump model must be supported without changing scoring for existing models. Batch training, incremental learning, dedicated builders, pipelines, monitoring, and delivery automation offer different balances of control, update speed, modularity, and operational effort. The design space does not guarantee a one-month delivery time.

options.name: Versioned batch learning with human review
pros: New training data triggers a repeatable training and validation pipeline.
Versioning, monitoring, and human review make updates easier to trace.
cons: Batch learning and human review slow adaptation and add manual work.
options.reason: Choose this for controlled updates and traceability with a relatively understandable workflow.

options.name: Event-driven hybrid learning with a builder component
pros: Hybrid learning can use findings promptly while retaining batch validation.
A dedicated builder and pipeline delivery support modular model changes.
cons: Automated adjustment, orchestration, and event infrastructure raise monitoring and maintenance demands.
options.reason: Choose this for stronger feedback speed and explicit model boundaries when automation can be governed.

options.name: Hybrid online and offline learning with automated delivery
pros: Hybrid learning and automated adjustment shorten the route from findings to prediction updates.
CI/CD and orchestration support repeatable work across model components.
cons: The combined modes and automation create significant coordination and control work.
options.reason: Choose this when flexible online and batch operation matters more than keeping the workflow small.

options.name: Manual scheduled batch workflow
pros: Minimizes automated infrastructure and may be familiar to a small team.
cons: Manual deployment and batch updates weaken new-model onboarding and feedback responsiveness.
options.reason: Set aside because it misses the modifiability scenario and offers slow feedback.

unaddressed.note: The space offers data storage patterns but no decision about physical hosting or premises ownership. Each alternative must separately deploy its storage and processing on utility premises to satisfy this constraint.
